bib.title: ImageNet Large Scale Visual Recognition Challenge

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "ImageNet Large Scale Visual Recognition Challenge", Russakovsky*, Deng*, Su, Krause, Satheesh, Ma, Huang, Karpathy, Khosla, Bernstein, Berg, Fei-Fei. IJCV 2015. The file is the arXiv version, 1409.0575v3, dated 30 Jan 2015.

COVERAGE: All 43 pages, 195,009 chars. I read the body, Tables 1–9, Appendices A–F and the bibliography. I only skimmed the class lists in App. A and App. D.

**Correct this in the notes before citing:** the paper never names Karpathy as an annotator. It reports "A1" and "A2". The "~5.1%" figure belongs to A1. Calling it "Karpathy's" error comes from outside this source.

CLAIMS
- claim: Winning top-5 classification error fell 4.2x over 2010–2014. The winners were 2010 NEC 28.2, 2011 XRCE 25.8, 2012 SuperVision 16.4, 2013 Clarifai 11.7 and 2014 GoogLeNet 6.7.
  number: 28.2% → 6.7%
  setup: provided-data entries only. Classes changed in 2010→11 and 2011→12, and the dataset has been fixed since 2012. With outside data, SuperVision got 15.3% and Clarifai 11.2%.
  quote: "There has been a 4.2x reduction in image classification error (from 28.2% to 6.7%) and a 1.7x reduction in single-object localization error (from 42.5% to 25.3%)"; "The dataset has not changed since 2012, and there has been a 2.4x reduction in image classification error (from 16.4% to 6.7%)"
  where: p.22–23 (§6.1.1); per-team numbers in Tables 5–7, pp.19–21
- claim: A trained annotator beat GoogLeNet by about 1.7 points on a 1,500-image test sample. A less-trained annotator did much worse, mostly because he missed the correct label.
  number: A1 5.1% vs GoogLeNet 6.8% (p=0.022); A2 12.0%
  setup: Random 1,500 images from the ILSVRC2012–14 test set, top-5. The labeling interface showed 1,000 classes, each with 13 example images. A1 trained on 500 images and labeled 1,500. A2 trained on 100 and labeled 258; GoogLeNet scored 5.8% on A2's subset. Pace was about 1 image per minute. The "optimistic" human (A1 or A2 correct) scored 2.4% vs GoogLeNet 4.9% on 204 shared images.
  quote: "The human error was estimated to be 5.1%. Thus, annotator A1 achieves a performance superior to GoogLeNet, by approximately 1.7%"; "final classification error is significantly worse, at approximately 12.0% Top-5 error. The majority of these errors (48.8%) can be attributed to the annotator failing to spot and consider the ground truth label"
  where: p.31 (§6.4.1, Table 9)
- claim: Humans and the model fail on different images. GoogLeNet misses small/thin objects, filtered photos and abstract depictions. Humans miss fine-grained classes and classes they do not know exist.
  number: GoogLeNet errors: 24% multiple objects, 21% small/thin, 13% filters, 6% abstract, 7% fine-grained. Human (A1) errors: 16% multiple objects, 37% fine-grained, 24% class unawareness, 5% insufficient examples.
  setup: Manual inspection of A1's 1,500 images.
  quote: "approximately 22 (21%) of GoogLeNet errors fall into this category, while none of the human errors do"; "We estimate that 28 (37%) of the human errors fall into this category, while only 7 (7%) of GoogLeNet errors do"
  where: p.31–33 (§6.4.2)
- claim: Dataset sizes. Classification and localization use 1,000 classes. Detection uses 200 classes.
  number: CLS 2012–14: 1,281,167 train / 50,000 val / 100,000 test. LOC: 523,966 train images with 593,173 boxes. DET 2014: 456,567 train / 21,121 val / 40,152 test, 478,807 train boxes.
  setup: Tables 2 and 4. The per-class train range for CLS is 732–1300.
  quote: "ILSVRC2012-14 1,281,167 (732-1300) 50,000 (50) 100,000 (100)"; "There are 200 object classes and approximately 450K training images, 20K validation images and 40K test images"
  where: p.9 (Table 2), p.14–15 (§3.3.4, Table 4)
- claim: Label quality is high but not perfect. About 0.3% of test labels are wrong, which puts a floor under measured error.
  number: 99.7% precision; 97.9% of images fully box-covered; 99.2% of boxes tight
  setup: Two checks. 80 synsets were sampled across all of ImageNet. Separately, 1,500 ILSVRC2012–14 test images were checked by hand. Boxes were evaluated on 10 categories with 200 images each.
  quote: "We found 5 annotation errors, corresponding as expected to 99.7% precision"; "97.9% images are completely covered with bounding boxes"
  where: p.7 (§3.1.3), p.9 (§3.2.1), p.32 (§6.4.2)
- claim: Detection mAP nearly doubled from 2013 to 2014. More training data explains only 1–4 points of that.
  number: 22.6% → 43.9% mAP
  setup: Same test set. The 2014 winner used outside data, namely the classification images. UvA's 2013 method gained 5.8 points from algorithm changes alone.
  quote: "all account for approximately 1−4% in absolute mAP improvement"
  where: p.23 (§6.1.2)

LIMITS
- The authors concede that test images carry only one label each, although many contain several objects. This is why scoring is top-5. "Multiple objects" accounts for 24% of GoogLeNet's errors (p.15, p.31–32).
- Labels for fine-grained classes are noisy because the annotators were non-experts (p.34).
- Criticisms they answer, in their own words: objects are "large and centered", there are annotation errors, and the rules on outside data are unclear (p.33–34).
- The human baseline is two annotators, both authors' colleagues. A2 covered only 258 images. A1's 1.7-point lead holds only at p=0.022.
- Even the best result for each class varies widely. Classification has a 41.0% accuracy range across classes, and the hardest class sits at 59.0% (p.24–25). In their words, the benchmark is "far from saturated".
- Not shown: robustness to distribution shift, segmentation, any comparison on harder tasks (they leave that open, p.33), and anything after 2014. This version predates ResNet (2015). Its human-vs-machine comparison is out of date, since later models pass 5.1%, but this paper does not show that.
- Dataset bias is mentioned only by pointing to Torralba & Efros 2011 (p.3). The paper itself does not analyze demographic or geographic bias.

BUILDS ON: PASCAL VOC (Everingham et al., 2010, IJCV; 2014 retrospective, IJCV), ImageNet (Deng et al., 2009, CVPR), WordNet (Miller, 1995, Commun. ACM), bounding-box crowdsourcing (Su et al., 2012, AAAI HCOMP workshop), multi-label annotation (Deng et al., 2014, CHI), AMT annotation (Sorokin and Forsyth, 2008), dataset bias (Torralba and Efros, 2011, CVPR), Krizhevsky et al., 2012 (NIPS), Szegedy et al., 2014 (tech report), and Simonyan and Zisserman, 2014 (CoRR).

CODE: none worth keeping. Eq. 5 (p.17) is the detection IoU threshold, relaxed for small objects, as printed: thr(B) = min(0.5, wh/((w+10)(h+10))). It changes the threshold for 5.5% of validation objects.

FIGURES: Fig. 9, p.23: "Performance of winning entries in the ILSVRC2010-2014 competitions in each of the three tasks". It shows the year-by-year error and mAP trend at a glance. Fig. 15, p.32 (common sources of error): representative human/GoogLeNet failure cases. These are good for the benchmark-reading section.

PROBLEMS: The text extracted cleanly. Some numbers came out with spaces inside them (e.g. "99 .7%"), which I removed in the quotes above. The figures.py captions command returned no output, so the figure pages above come from the running page headers in the text. I found no embedded instructions.
